title: Can we safeguard our constitution before the next general election?
gist: Writing days after Andy Burnham became UK prime minister on 20th July 2026, a lawyer-columnist argues the current parliament (403 Labour MPs, a possible run to August 2029) is a once-in-a-generation window to hard-wire constitutional checks before a plausibly 'radically illiberal' successor government, and that the UCL Constitution Unit's new Safeguarding the Constitution paper is only a partial fix because its 'soft' proposals (reviews, transparency) can be swept away instantly.

themes.theme: UK parliamentary arithmetic as a closing window

insights.claim: The UK parliament elected two years ago could run until summer 2029, with the next general election legally due no later than 15th August 2029, though new prime minister Andy Burnham could call one sooner.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Sets the outer bound on UK political risk timing: up to three more years of Labour-majority policymaking, with early-election optionality held by the new PM.
insights.locator: Currently, there is a parliament which could last

insights.claim: Andy Burnham became UK prime minister on 20th July 2026, replacing the previous leadership within the same parliament rather than via a general election.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A mid-parliament PM change resets UK policy expectations without a fresh mandate — watch for early-election speculation as a gilt and sterling risk factor.
insights.locator: Andy Burnham speaks in Downing Street after becoming prime minister

insights.claim: The current House of Commons contains 403 Labour MPs, 71 Liberal Democrats, 12 Scottish and Welsh nationalists, five Greens and two SDLP, against a rump of 117 Conservatives, seven Reform and five DUP, giving a nominally left-of-centre bloc an unprecedented majority for fundamental constitutional reform.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Quantifies how little parliamentary friction exists in the UK right now — legislation risk (in either direction) is bounded only by government will, not by opposition arithmetic.
insights.quote: Never in recent history has there been such a potential majority for fundamental constitutional reform.
insights.locator: There are currently 403 Labour members of parliament

insights.claim: Even a House of Lords veto could be overridden in this parliament because there is still time to deploy the Parliament Acts, removing the upper chamber as a practical constraint on constitutional legislation.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The Lords is a delay mechanism, not a blocker, and only while enough parliamentary time remains — timing, not composition, is the binding constraint.
insights.locator: And nor would the House of Lords

insights.claim: The best moment to build institutional safeguards is while political conditions are calm and a compliant majority exists, not when the threat has already arrived — the constitutional analogue of fixing a roof while the sun shines.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A general timing heuristic for institutional and governance risk: safeguards priced cheaply in calm periods become unbuyable once regime risk is visible.
insights.quote: There is an old English saying, dating from the 16th century: to make hay while the sun shines.
insights.locator: There is an old English saying

insights.claim: The window for pre-emptive UK constitutional reform is described as a once-in-a-political-generation opportunity that is nonetheless likely to be wasted.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Base case is inaction, so do not price in stronger UK institutional guardrails when modelling medium-term policy volatility.
insights.quote: We have a once-in-a-political-generation opportunity to force through change, even if that opportunity is likely to be wasted.

insights.claim: There is a non-trivial probability that the composition of the House of Commons is radically different after the next UK general election, because radically illiberal parties in the United States and continental Europe have proved highly effective at both gaining and retaining power.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Treat a discontinuous UK political regime change by 2029 as a live tail scenario rather than a fringe one when sizing long-duration UK exposure.

insights.claim: The UK's uncodified constitution contains almost nothing capable of stopping a determined and considered assault on the checks and balances constraining raw executive power, so those arrangements could buckle quickly under a radically illiberal majority.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: UK institutional risk is structurally higher than its stable reputation implies — rule-of-law premia embedded in UK asset pricing may be too low.
insights.quote: There is very little in our constitution which would be able to stop a determined and considered assault on the checks and balances to raw executive power.
insights.locator: And if there is a radically illiberal majority

insights.claim: The Reform party's leader is currently having a hard time politically, but the underlying support he and others are exploiting will persist regardless of his personal fortunes.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Don't read a single populist leader's slump as decay of the populist vote bloc — the demand side outlives the personality supplying it.
insights.quote: The leader of the Reform party, a supreme political opportunist, may be having a hard time at the moment, but the political support he and others are exploiting will still be there.
insights.locator: A glance at the United States

insights.claim: Previous columns in this series flagged the possibility of an Enabling Act in the UK, framing the risk as a legislature voluntarily handing sweeping powers to the executive rather than an external coup.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: The mechanism to monitor is delegation of power by consent — statutory instruments and enabling clauses, not dramatic constitutional ruptures.
insights.locator: as set out in previous Weekly Constitutional columns

insights.claim: Future observers may look back on this period and ask why so little was done to anticipate an illiberal turn, implying institutional complacency is the central failure mode rather than lack of warning.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Complacency risk is the tell: institutions that look robust because they have never been tested are the ones to underwrite most carefully.
insights.quote: Our constitutional arrangements are vulnerable and it is complacent to think otherwise.
insights.locator: There is a risk that one day we shall look back

themes.theme: Hard vs soft safeguards: the UCL Constitution Unit paper

insights.claim: The Constitution Unit at University College London published a paper titled Safeguarding the Constitution: Key Steps to Strengthen UK Democratic Resilience whose scope is narrower than its title, addressing the parliamentary system rather than judicial protection of human rights or citizens' ability to challenge government abuses in court.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated policy document to track as the reform menu any UK government would draw from — and a marker of what reform advocates are not asking for.
insights.quote: The title is ambitious and wide-ranging
insights.locator: there was an interesting paper published this week

insights.claim: Constitutional safeguards can be sorted into 'hard' ones, where an actor inside the polity can say no to the government and be obeyed, and 'soft' ones such as reviews, transparency and expert input that depend on the government's continued goodwill.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A transferable test for any governance or regulatory regime: only veto rights with teeth survive a hostile administration, so discount 'transparency' commitments.
insights.locator: Some of these proposals are what could be called

insights.claim: The genuinely hard proposals on the table are requiring parliamentary consent before prorogation or dissolution, giving MPs more control over parliamentary process, and putting ethics regulators on a statutory footing the government cannot simply remove.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: These are the specific, checkable legislative markers that would signal real UK institutional hardening rather than cosmetic reform.
insights.locator: making it so that parliament must give consent

insights.claim: The negative procedure that lets statutory instruments and codes of practice become law without a meaningful vote is described as much-abused, yet the paper proposes only a review of the delegated legislation system rather than abolishing it.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Delegated legislation is where UK regulatory change actually happens with least scrutiny — the channel to monitor for abrupt rule changes affecting businesses.
insights.locator: There should be a mere “review” of the delegated legislation system

insights.claim: Soft safeguards fail on two counts: there is probably not enough time before the next general election to convert reviews into implemented proposals, and transparency and expertise can be swept away easily by an incoming illiberal government.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Reform proposals that require multi-year review pipelines are effectively null in a compressed political window — judge them on implementation lag.
insights.locator: The problems with such soft proposals are twofold

insights.claim: The United States has a far stronger freedom of information regime than the United Kingdom and it has done little good, showing that formal transparency rights are weak protection against executive overreach.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Discount disclosure-based governance protections when assessing political risk; enforcement power, not information access, is what binds.
insights.quote: The United States, for example, has a far stronger freedom of information regime than the United Kingdom, for all the good it has done.

insights.claim: The new nominally left-wing UK government is in practice illiberal and arguably repressive on immigration and other matters, having kept Shabana Mahmood at the Home Office while sacking Lord Timpson as prisons minister.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Personnel choices, not party labels, are the read on UK immigration and criminal-justice policy direction — a continuity signal for restrictive policy and prison capacity spend.
insights.locator: The new prime minister has kept Shabana Mahmood

insights.claim: On policy substance the present UK administration is arguably indistinguishable from a Conservative-Reform coalition, meaning a change of governing party may not change the policy trajectory that matters to markets.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: If policy convergence is real, UK election outcomes matter less for sector policy than for institutional-quality risk — trade the institutions, not the party.
insights.quote: There is a case that in policy the present administration is indistinguishable from a Conservative-Reform administration.
insights.locator: Many from a liberal perspective would rightly dispute
